supported_claims.text: 水 is an indivisible pictograph of flowing water: early forms show a central current with side marks representing droplets. The character’s visible parts are features of the whole picture, not separate components.

The earliest cited attestations are Shang oracle-bone examples used for water or flooding; the cited examples are not individually dated. Bronze and Warring States forms are described as continuing the flowing-water picture.
The current common meaning is water; the dossier also records the glosses liquid, lotion and juice, but those glosses alone do not establish a historical sequence.

A bronze inscription is reported to use 水 to write 乞, ‘request.’ This is a proposed graph borrowing: the sign was reused for a different word, not shown to have acquired that meaning through semantic development.
The dossier reports 水準 for a leveling instrument and a later abstract sense ‘standard’ or ‘level,’ but supplies no dated attestations for these stages.

disagreements.text: The Shuowen passage gives a Han-era gloss and cosmological account, while the cited palaeographic analysis treats the graph as a flowing-water picture and interprets the gloss as phonetic glossing. The Shuowen account is historical interpretation, not independent proof of the graph’s original formation.
One reported oracle-bone use is disputed: proposed readings connect it to leveling land with water or washing a temple, and its relation to the ordinary water noun is unresolved.
Proposed comparisons for the spoken word 水 and competing Old Chinese reconstructions remain unresolved in this dossier; they do not establish a sound component in the character.

limitations.text: No distinct internal component split or phonetic component is supported; the character is analyzed as a whole pictograph.
The bronze graph-borrowing example is reported, but the research did not independently establish a historical sound match between 水 and 乞.
The individual oracle-bone examples are not dated in the cited account, and no artifact image was visually inspected; the selected oracle and bronze glyphs are modern vector redrawings.
